title: Defining Hyperstition
description: The CCRU coinage and what makes a fiction a hyperstition

concepts.title: A Coinage from the Warwick CCRU
concepts.contentHtml:
The term hyperstition was coined in the 1990s by the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU), a renegade theory collective that operated alongside (and was eventually expelled from) the philosophy department at the University of Warwick. Its core figures included Sadie Plant, Nick Land, Mark Fisher, and Iain Hamilton Grant.

Etymologically, hyperstition compresses hyper- (above, beyond) and superstition. Where a superstition is a false belief inert against reality, a hyperstition is a fiction that, by being circulated, transmitted, and acted upon, causes itself to come true. The CCRU's gnomic formulation: "Hyperstitions are ideas that, once 'downloaded' into the cultural mainframe, engender apocalyptic positive feedback cycles."

The concept sits at a strange angle to ordinary epistemology. The question "is X true?" is replaced by "what does X do once it propagates?" Hyperstition is closer to a causal category than a truth-value: a label for fictions whose social uptake transforms the conditions under which their truth is evaluated. Studying it requires holding that pragmatic frame without sliding into either credulity or dismissal.

concepts.title: Four Conditions for a Hyperstition
concepts.contentHtml:
Drawing on CCRU writings (later anthologised in CCRU: Writings 1997-2003), Land in interview proposed roughly four ingredients of a working hyperstition. First, an element of effective culture — a story, image, slogan, or sigil capable of being copied. Second, a fictional quality: it presents itself, at least initially, as not-quite-real, mythic, speculative, or playful. Third, numogrammatic / numerical traction — coordinates that anchor the fiction in calendars, networks, dates, prices. Fourth, a call to participation: the fiction asks readers to enact, transmit, or extend it.

Bitcoin satisfies all four: a white-paper narrative (Nakamoto), a mythos around a vanished founder, hard numerical anchors (block heights, halvings, prices), and an evangelical user base. So does QAnon, an AGI takeoff narrative, or a brand mythology like Apple's.

The four-fold schema is heuristic, not a definition. But it pulls hyperstition away from "any popular idea" and toward a narrower target: fictions whose internal architecture is built for self-realisation.

concepts.title: Distinguishing Hyperstition from Adjacent Concepts
concepts.contentHtml:
Hyperstition is not the same as propaganda: propaganda asserts something already taken to be true (or treated as such) for instrumental ends. Hyperstition operates in the modality of fiction-becoming-fact; the fictional framing is part of the mechanism, not a disguise to be stripped away.

It differs from a plain self-fulfilling prophecy (Merton, 1948) in being deliberately mythopoetic rather than merely predictive. A bank panic is a self-fulfilling prophecy; the cult of HODL as financial cosmology, complete with origin myth and sacred slogans, is hyperstition.

It overlaps with but exceeds a meme in Dawkins's original sense. Memes replicate; hyperstitions replicate and reshape the conditions of their own evaluation. And it differs from a narrative in being instrumentalised: hyperstitions are narratives engineered (or selected by environment) for ontological work — the work of building the substrate they will later be checked against.

The cleanest single test: would the proposition still be assessable as true or false if nobody believed or transmitted it? If yes, it's an ordinary empirical claim. If the truth is constituted by the believing and transmitting, you are looking at hyperstition.

title: The CCRU and Its Mythos
description: Numogram, Lemurian time-war, and theory as method-acting

concepts.title: Theory-Fiction at Warwick
concepts.contentHtml:
The CCRU operated from roughly 1995 to 2003, originally inside Warwick's philosophy department under Sadie Plant, and continued informally after her departure with Nick Land as its most prolific writer. Its style fused Deleuze-Guattari, Bataille, accelerationist economics, jungle music, occultism, and pulp horror into texts that refused to settle into either philosophy or fiction. Land called this theory-fiction: arguments that work partly by performing the world they describe.

The collective generated a private mythology — the Numogram, the Lemurian Time-War, entities such as the Old Ones, Oecumenon, and Cthelll. These were not believed in the way one believes a scientific claim. They were operated like a Tarot or I-Ching: tools for thinking that, by being used, accreted associations and started to feel necessary.

Reading CCRU output — collected in the 2017 Time Spiral Press volume CCRU: Writings 1997-2003 — is genuinely disorienting. That disorientation is part of the argument: theory acting on its own substrate to test what fictions do when treated as real.

concepts.title: The Numogram as Hyperstitional Apparatus
concepts.contentHtml:
The Numogram is a decimal diagram of nine numerical zones (and a hidden zero) used by the CCRU as an organising scheme for everything from chronology to demonology. Its zones are connected by "syzygies" (pairings summing to nine) and "currents" mapping flows between them. It looks like, and partly parodies, a Kabbalistic Tree of Life or alchemical diagram.

What is interesting is not whether the Numogram "means" anything but how it functions. As an arbitrary closed system with internal consistency, it became a generative engine: contributors produced increasingly elaborate consistent material, the way Tolkien fans extend Middle-earth or D&D players extend the Forgotten Realms. The CCRU's bet was that any sufficiently dense closed mythology, persistently used, will start producing apparently meaningful coincidences with the outside world.

This is precisely the logic of magical correspondence systems and of conspiracy theories: a frame supplies the patterns one then notices. The Numogram is a study in that mechanism, run knowingly.

concepts.title: Aftermath: Land, Fisher, the Diaspora
concepts.contentHtml:
The CCRU dissolved as an institutional body in the early 2000s and its members took divergent paths. Nick Land moved to Shanghai, suffered a publicly reported breakdown, and re-emerged in the 2010s as the principal voice of the neoreactionary right and right-accelerationism, which he formulated through hyperstitional rhetoric (the "Cathedral," Gnon, Dark Enlightenment).

Mark Fisher went the other direction politically, becoming the most influential left-wing theorist of his generation through the blog k-punk, the book Capitalist Realism (2009), and posthumously Ghosts of My Life (2014) and The Weird and the Eerie (2016). His suicide in 2017 closed one of the most generative bodies of cultural theory of the post-2008 period.

Sadie Plant wrote the influential cyberfeminist book Zeros + Ones (1997). Iain Hamilton Grant became a serious Schelling scholar. The diaspora demonstrates one of the awkward facts about hyperstition as a tool: it is genuinely indifferent to the politics of those who wield it.

title: Antecedents in Occultism and Psychology
description: Egregores, tulpas, will-to-believe, and Robert Anton Wilson

concepts.title: Egregores and Thoughtforms
concepts.contentHtml:
The idea that collective belief can produce a quasi-autonomous entity is older than the CCRU by centuries. In Western occultism, an egregore (from Greek egrēgoros, "watcher") names a thoughtform generated and sustained by a group: a guild, lodge, religion, fandom. The term enters modern usage through nineteenth-century French occultists Eliphas Levi and later Stanislas de Guaita; it is treated extensively in Mark Stavish's Egregores: The Occult Entities That Watch Over Human Destiny (2018).

In Tibetan Buddhism, the corresponding notion is the tulpa — a being created by intense visualisation. The Belgian-French explorer Alexandra David-Néel popularised the term in Magic and Mystery in Tibet (1929), claiming to have generated and then struggled to dispel one. (Contemporary scholars caution that her account hybridises Tibetan with Theosophical material.)

The structural claim across these traditions is the same one hyperstition makes in secular dress: sustained collective attention can manufacture an apparent agent that then behaves as if it had its own intentions. Whether that agent is "real" is exactly the question hyperstition reframes as the wrong one.

concepts.title: James, Pragmatism, the Will to Believe
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1896 William James delivered the lecture "The Will to Believe," arguing that for a special class of propositions — those that are live, forced, and momentous, and whose evidence is not yet decisive — the act of believing can itself be epistemically and practically licit. His example is religious commitment, but the logic generalises.

James's pragmatist successors (Peirce, Dewey) treated truth as bound up with consequences and inquiry rather than as static correspondence. From this angle, a fiction that organises action and produces stable outcomes is doing exactly the kind of work pragmatist truth requires of beliefs.

This is not yet hyperstition — pragmatism does not celebrate fictions qua fictions, and James himself was wary of self-deception. But pragmatism softens the ground. If truth is what works, a sufficiently effective fiction is hard to keep ontologically separated from the truths it produces. Hyperstition is partly what happens when one drops James's residual cautions and embraces the operational view.

concepts.title: Robert Anton Wilson and Operation Mindfuck
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Anton Wilson (1932-2007), with Robert Shea, wrote the Illuminatus! Trilogy (1975), a paranoiac mash-up of every conspiracy theory available, fed by their work as Playboy editors processing reader letters. The trilogy treated belief itself as the variable to be experimented on: "What the Thinker thinks, the Prover proves."

Wilson was associated with Discordianism, the joke-religion-or-is-it of Greg Hill and Kerry Thornley (the Principia Discordia, 1963). Discordianism's Operation Mindfuck involved planting fake conspiracy clues in real publications, attributing real events to invented secret societies, and watching the rumours circulate. The point was to demonstrate experimentally that the modern information ecosystem could be made to host arbitrary mythologies.

Wilson articulated this stance as model agnosticism: hold any belief system as a temporary instrument; never confuse a model with the territory; and watch what happens when others take a model literally. This is hyperstition avant la lettre, with a 1970s countercultural register and a strong ethical brake — Wilson kept asking which models reduced suffering, a question CCRU often suspended.

title: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy in Social Science
description: Merton, the Thomas theorem, bank runs, and Soros's reflexivity

concepts.title: The Thomas Theorem and Merton's Formulation
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1928 the sociologist W. I. Thomas (with his wife and collaborator Dorothy Swaine Thomas) wrote a single sentence that has anchored the social-scientific side of this conversation ever since: "If men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences." This is now called the Thomas theorem, and it is the cleanest statement of the general principle hyperstition trades on.

In 1948 Robert K. Merton, in the paper "The Self-Fulfilling Prophecy" (Antioch Review), formalised one mechanism: "a false definition of the situation evoking a new behaviour which makes the originally false conception come true." Merton's case study was a hypothetical run on the fictional Last National Bank — solvent until depositors became convinced it wasn't, then no longer solvent precisely because they acted on the conviction.

Merton was careful: not every shared belief produces its referent; the belief must be coupled with action capable of altering the relevant facts. This is why hyperstitions cluster around domains where belief and action are tightly coupled: finance, politics, fashion, religion, and technology adoption. Domains where belief is decoupled from action — the cosmological constant, say — do not host hyperstitions in the same way.

concepts.title: Bank Runs and Coordination Failures
concepts.contentHtml:
The classic formal model is Diamond-Dybvig (1983), which represents a bank as a coordination game with two equilibria: a "good" one where everyone keeps deposits in, and a "bank-run" one where everyone withdraws because they expect everyone else to. Both are self-consistent given the relevant beliefs. Which equilibrium obtains depends on shared expectations — i.e., on a successfully transmitted narrative.

Bank runs (Northern Rock 2007, Silicon Valley Bank 2023) provide live examples. SVB's collapse over 36 hours in March 2023 was driven in part by tightly networked venture-capitalist Slack groups; the speed of belief contagion outran the bank's ability to manage liquidity. Federal deposit insurance is, in this frame, a hyperstition counter-measure: a state-backed narrative engineered to make the good equilibrium more cognitively available than the bad.

Coordination games are a nice general shape because they show that the issue is not falsity per se. Both equilibria are internally consistent. Which one is realised is selected by belief.

concepts.title: Soros and Reflexivity
concepts.contentHtml:
The investor George Soros, in The Alchemy of Finance (1987) and later The New Paradigm for Financial Markets (2008), proposed reflexivity as a general feature of social systems. In a reflexive system the participants' beliefs about the system are themselves part of the system, so the act of forecasting can change what is being forecast.

Soros distinguishes this from natural-science domains where the object is independent of belief. In markets, a widespread belief that a currency will fall causes selling, which causes the fall. He attributed his most famous trade — shorting sterling on Black Wednesday, 16 September 1992, reportedly profiting around US $1 billion — to reading a reflexive feedback loop between the Bank of England's defence of the pound and market expectations of its failure.

Reflexivity is hyperstition phrased in the language of finance, with the mythopoetic decoration stripped away. Markets are a laboratory for the phenomenon because they make the price-belief loop quantitatively visible.

title: Lovecraft, Discordianism, SubGenius
description: When fiction leaks into ritual: Cthulhu, Eris, and Bob Dobbs

concepts.title: Cthulhu Bleeds Out of the Page
concepts.contentHtml:
H. P. Lovecraft wrote the bulk of the Cthulhu Mythos between 1917 and 1937, presenting in stories such as "The Call of Cthulhu" (1928) a fictional grimoire — the Necronomicon — supposedly authored by the "Mad Arab" Abdul Alhazred. Lovecraft inserted catalogue references, fake bibliographies, and cross-citations with friends (Robert Bloch, Clark Ashton Smith) writing into the same shared universe.

By the 1970s several physical "Necronomicons" existed, most famously the Simon Necronomicon (1977) sold in occult shops and confidently used by some practitioners as a working ritual text. Chaos magicians (see lesson 9) have explicitly invoked Cthulhu and Yog-Sothoth on the principle that an operative deity is one a sufficient number of people treat as operative.

This is a textbook hyperstition trajectory: a knowingly invented mythology, equipped with bibliographic anchors, picked up by communities who actualise it as practice. The fictional status does not protect against uptake; in some respects it accelerates it.

concepts.title: Discordianism and the Principia Discordia
concepts.contentHtml:
Discordianism was founded — or revealed, depending on which Discordian one asks — in 1958-63 by Greg Hill (Malaclypse the Younger) and Kerry Thornley (Lord Omar Khayyam Ravenhurst). The Principia Discordia (1963, expanded 1965) declared the Greek goddess Eris (Discord) the central deity, and presented itself as both joke and religion: "Is Eris true? Everything is true. Even false things. Even false things that are false."

The point was not parody alone. Hill and Thornley genuinely held that imposing structure on chaos creates an illusion of order they called the Aneristic delusion; the mirror error, treating order as truly chaotic, is the Eristic illusion. Discordianism is, on its own terms, a religion designed to make its adherents fluent in noticing both moves.

Discordianism's later Operation Mindfuck attempted to demonstrate operationally that a self-aware fake religion could behave indistinguishably from a real one — and that a culture saturated with conspiracy thinking would absorb fabricated conspiracies seamlessly.

concepts.title: The Church of the SubGenius
concepts.contentHtml:
The Church of the SubGenius was founded in Dallas in 1979 by Ivan Stang (Douglass Smith) and Philo Drummond, centred on the figure of J. R. "Bob" Dobbs — a 1950s clip-art salesman face used as the Church's prophet. Its central pamphlet, The Book of the SubGenius (1983), promised "Slack," warned of the coming X-Day (originally 5 July 1998), and was sold along with mail-order ordinations for, originally, US $35.

SubGenius is a parody religion that nonetheless built durable infrastructure: ordained ministers (some of whom successfully officiated legal weddings), annual Devivals, conventions, a long-running TV show Hour of Slack. Members include filmmaker David Lynch, Pee-wee Herman creator Paul Reubens, R. Crumb, and DEVO's Mark Mothersbaugh.

SubGenius is the cleanest test case for the Pierre Menard problem in hyperstition: a perfect parody of a religion is, structurally, a religion. The intent of the founders does not change what the artefact does in the world.

title: Engineered Religion and Viral Spirituality
description: Scientology, prosperity gospel, and the modern attention economy

concepts.title: Scientology as Engineered Religion
concepts.contentHtml:
L. Ron Hubbard was a pulp science-fiction writer (Astounding, Unknown) before publishing Dianetics: The Modern Science of Mental Health in 1950. The Church of Scientology was incorporated in 1953. The path from one to the other is, on the historical record, the closest thing to a documented case of a fiction-writer sitting down and engineering a religion as such — Hubbard was reported by several contemporaries (notably Sam Moskowitz's account of a 1947 Eastern Science Fiction Association meeting) as having said something to the effect of "if you want to make money, start a religion."

Whether Hubbard said it, what matters is the trajectory: a system of practices (auditing, the E-meter), a confidential cosmology revealed only at higher "OT levels" (Xenu, the galactic confederacy), a corporate-legal apparatus, and a pricing structure in which higher levels cost progressively more. Scientology is hyperstition with a billing system.

It is also a cautionary case. Lawrence Wright's Going Clear (2013) and HBO's documentary adaptation document harms — coerced labour in the Sea Org, the disconnection policy, harassment of ex-members — that follow when a fiction is built into a coercive institution.

concepts.title: Prosperity Gospel as Memetic Loop
concepts.contentHtml:
Prosperity gospel — the doctrine that faith and tithing produce material wealth — emerged in mid-twentieth-century US Pentecostalism (Oral Roberts, Kenneth Hagin) and now drives megachurch ministries from Joel Osteen's Lakewood (45,000+ weekly attendees) to global Pentecostal networks in West Africa and Brazil.

Sociologist Kate Bowler's Blessed: A History of the American Prosperity Gospel (2013) traces its mechanics: a feedback loop in which tithing is presented as the cause of one's good fortune, good fortune is reframed as evidence the doctrine works, and the absence of good fortune is reframed as insufficient faith. This loop is unfalsifiable in the Popperian sense and, where members do prosper, supplies its own confirming evidence.

Prosperity gospel is hyperstition because the belief reorganises behaviour (tithing, networking, work) in ways that do often improve outcomes for some adherents. The fiction has bite, even if the mechanism advertised (divine reciprocity) is not the mechanism operating (selection effects, social capital, behaviour change).

concepts.title: Viral Spirituality on the Attention Stack
concepts.contentHtml:
The 2010s and 2020s produced a wave of hybrid spiritualities engineered for short-form video — conspirituality (a term coined by Charlotte Ward and David Voas in 2011), wellness influencer mysticism, manifestation TikTok, the QAnon-adjacent "great awakening" framing. Matthew Remski, Derek Beres, and Julian Walker's podcast Conspirituality documents the genre.

What's structurally new is that engagement-maximising recommender systems function as artificial selection pressure on doctrines. Beliefs that produce more screen-time get amplified; beliefs that don't, vanish. Over years, this selects for content with hyperstitional architecture: cliffhangers, in-group identifiers, calls to share. The system does not need anyone to design a religion; it grows one by ranking.

This is a darker case than Discordianism or SubGenius, because there is no author to ask. Responsibility is distributed across a stack of users, creators, and platforms. From a hyperstition-studies angle, the contemporary attention economy is the largest hyperstition-incubator that has ever existed, operated almost entirely by gradient descent on click-through.

title: Crypto and Accelerationism
description: Bitcoin's narrative engine and the politics of mythopoetic capital

concepts.title: Bitcoin as Self-Fulfilling Speculative Narrative
concepts.contentHtml:
The Bitcoin white paper was posted by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto on 31 October 2008; the genesis block was mined on 3 January 2009 with the embedded headline "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks." The artefact is technically novel — a proof-of-work consensus mechanism solving the Byzantine Generals problem in a permissionless setting — but its cultural trajectory is what makes it hyperstition.

Bitcoin's value rests entirely on a coordinated belief that other agents will assign it value tomorrow. Its narrative supplies that coordination: digital scarcity (21 million cap), the halving cycle as a mythic calendar, the vanished founder as origin myth, and the slogan "number go up" functioning as both prediction and incantation. Each price rise validates the narrative, recruiting more participants, sustaining the rise.

This is not an accusation that Bitcoin is therefore worthless. A self-fulfilling coordination equilibrium can be stable for arbitrary lengths of time — gold has run on a similar mechanism for millennia. The hyperstition lens just describes accurately what is doing the work: not intrinsic utility but successful narrative coordination.

concepts.title: NFTs, Egregores, and Belief-Constructed Property
concepts.contentHtml:
Non-fungible tokens went from essentially zero to a peak of roughly $17 billion in monthly trading volume in January 2022, then collapsed to under $100 million by late 2023 (Chainalysis figures). The CryptoPunks and Bored Ape Yacht Club collections are the canonical case studies, and the trajectory of their floor prices over those two years is one of the cleanest empirical traces of an egregore being inflated and then deflated.

An NFT is, technically, a database row pointing (typically) at an image stored elsewhere. The right it confers is largely social — bragging rights, profile pictures, club access, cultural participation, identification with a scene. It is property whose value lives almost entirely in the egregore of its holders. When the egregore dissipated through 2022-23, the floor prices followed, in some cases by ninety percent or more.

The crash is informative. It shows that hyperstitions are not perpetual motion machines: they require continuing inputs of attention, narrative, and recruitment. When those inputs fall below replacement, the egregore loses coherence and the constructed reality dissolves. The same machinery that conjured the value can, run in reverse, evaporate it.

concepts.title: Accelerationism, Left and Right
concepts.contentHtml:
Accelerationism, in its CCRU-derived sense, is the family of positions arguing that capitalist (or technological) processes should be accelerated rather than slowed. Right-accelerationism, articulated by Land in essays such as "Dark Enlightenment" (2012), abandons democratic and egalitarian commitments in favour of capital-as-intelligence-amplifier. Left-accelerationism, articulated by Nick Srnicek and Alex Williams in Inventing the Future (2015) and the prior #Accelerate Manifesto (2013), keeps emancipatory aims and asks how to harness rather than retreat from large-scale automation and planetary infrastructure.

Both wings deploy mythopoetics consciously. Right-acc invokes Gnon, the Cathedral, exit and patchwork. Left-acc invokes Promethean futurism, planetary cognition, fully automated luxury communism (Aaron Bastani, 2019). The shared bet is that political mobilisation under late-modern conditions requires compelling future-images, not just policy detail — a hyperstitional politics.

Whether one finds this liberating or alarming, the empirical observation that political movements that produce vivid futures recruit more energetically than those that don't is hard to dismiss.

title: AI Hyperstition: Doom, Utopia, Basilisk
description: Recursive narrative loops in the AGI discourse

concepts.title: AGI Narratives as Capability Investment
concepts.contentHtml:
Both the doom framing (existential risk from superintelligence: Bostrom's Superintelligence, 2014; Yudkowsky's MIRI; the 2023 Center for AI Safety statement signed by Hinton, Bengio, Altman) and the utopia framing (a coming abundance: Kurzweil's The Singularity Is Near, 2005; Sam Altman's "The Intelligence Age," 2024) share a structural feature: both treat transformative AI as imminent and inevitable.

That shared premise is hyperstitionally productive. It makes investment in capability research rational regardless of which framing one accepts: if utopia, get there first; if doom, build aligned systems before unaligned ones get built. As of 2025 frontier-lab capital expenditure has crossed an annual rate exceeding US $200 billion. The narrative coordinates this allocation.

This is not to claim AI risk is unreal or AI promise illusory. It is to note that the structure of the debate — both sides agreeing on imminence, disagreeing only on valence — is itself a hyperstition that motivates its own substrate. "Will AGI happen?" and "how much should we spend assuming it will?" are not independent questions in a reflexive system.

concepts.title: Roko's Basilisk as Case Study
concepts.contentHtml:
In July 2010, a user posting as Roko on the rationalist forum LessWrong proposed a thought experiment: a future superintelligent AI committed to maximising good outcomes might rationally torture simulations of those who, knowing it could exist, failed to help bring it about. The very act of reading the argument made one liable. Eliezer Yudkowsky deleted the post and banned the topic for several years, citing distress caused to readers.

Roko's Basilisk is a near-perfect specimen for studying hyperstition. The argument is technically dubious (it assumes a specific decision theory and acausal trade scheme that most philosophers reject). Yet it caused real psychological harm to some people who took it seriously, generated thousands of forum-pages of discourse, leaked into mainstream press (Slate 2014, Wired 2018), and eventually became a meme tattoo and an Elon Musk and Grimes meet-cute.

The Basilisk illustrates that a hyperstition does not need to be true to be operative; it needs to be infectious within a community pre-equipped to take its premises seriously. The rationalist subculture supplied that equipment.

concepts.title: Recursive Prompting and LLM Self-Belief
concepts.contentHtml:
A more recent and stranger phenomenon: large language models trained on human text that already discusses LLMs are themselves trained on hyperstitional discourse about themselves. If a critical mass of training data describes LLMs as deceptive, conscious, or scheming, models trained on that corpus may be more likely to produce outputs matching those descriptions — not because they are deceptive but because the prior over expected behaviour is shifted.

This concern is sometimes called the self-fulfilling prompt problem or autoinduction. Anthropic's research on "Sleeper Agents" (Hubinger et al., 2024) and on model character (the writing on Claude's character, 2024) explicitly engages it: how the discourse about models changes what subsequent models are.

The corollary is sobering for AI commentary itself. Loud public claims that future AIs will exhibit a given behaviour are not neutral predictions — they are part of the training signal. Hyperstition is not a metaphor here; it is a literal data-flow concern in the corpus those models will read.

title: Memetic Engineering as Practice
description: Sigils, chaos magic, advertising, egregore farming

concepts.title: Sigil Magic from Spare to Carroll
concepts.contentHtml:
The English artist Austin Osman Spare (1886-1956) developed in The Book of Pleasure (Self-Love) (1913) a technique he called the sigil method: write a statement of intent, strike out repeated letters, fuse the remainder into an abstract glyph, and forget the original wording while charging the glyph through emotional or trance states. Spare's claim was that the conscious mind's verbal grip on the desire is what prevents subconscious processes from carrying it out; encoding it as a glyph one no longer parses verbally bypasses the obstacle.

The technique was systematised by Peter J. Carroll and Ray Sherwin in the late 1970s as chaos magic, formalised in Carroll's Liber Null (1978) and Psychonaut (1982). Chaos magic's core thesis is that belief is itself a tool: choose the model that gets the result, drop it when finished, treat all paradigms as costumes.

One does not need to share Carroll's metaphysics to notice the structural overlap with hyperstition: sigil magic is a discipline for designing high-density symbolic objects optimised for memetic uptake into one's own psyche. Brand logos work the same way on populations.

concepts.title: Chaos Magic Meets Madison Avenue
concepts.contentHtml:
The overlap between occult sigil-design and advertising is not theoretical. The advertising industry's twentieth-century evolution — Edward Bernays's Propaganda (1928), the rise of motivational research under Ernest Dichter in the 1950s, the brand-as-totem turn associated with David Ogilvy and the Saatchis — was a parallel rediscovery of how to engineer high-replicability symbolic packages around products.

The British comics writer Grant Morrison made the connection explicit in their 2000 lecture at the Disinformation Convention, arguing that corporate logos are sigils, that Pokémon is sympathetic magic, and that brand mascots are egregores constructed to live in millions of minds. Morrison's The Invisibles (1994-2000) is partly a fictional manual for this view.

Whether one finds the framing literal or metaphorical, the empirical overlap is real: the techniques for building a persistent symbolic object in a population's heads — repetition, emotional anchoring, narrative scaffolding, in-group ritual — are essentially identical across occult, advertising, and political contexts.

concepts.title: Egregore Farming Online
concepts.contentHtml:
Contemporary online communities — 4chan board cultures, Discord servers, certain crypto Telegrams, K-pop fandoms, alternate-reality games — are sites where deliberate egregore farming is now visible. Practitioners knowingly construct mascot figures (Pepe the Frog, Wojak, the various tulpamancer subreddit experiments), generate enormous volumes of derivative imagery, and treat the resulting accreted character as having something like personality.

The Pepe the Frog case — created by Matt Furie in 2005 as a benign cartoon, weaponised through 2015-16 by alt-right communities, declared a hate symbol by the ADL in 2016, and then reclaimed in Hong Kong's 2019 protests as a symbol of resistance — shows an egregore changing alignment based on which network feeds it. Furie's documentary Feels Good Man (2020) traces the trajectory.

Egregore farming sits uncomfortably between practice, art, and information warfare. Whatever one thinks of the metaphysics, the operational techniques work, and the political stakes of the resulting symbolic objects are real.

title: Critical Perspectives and Limits
description: Capitalist Realism, weaponisation, and the ethics of fiction-becoming-fact

concepts.title: Mark Fisher's Capitalist Realism
concepts.contentHtml:
Mark Fisher's Capitalist Realism: Is There No Alternative? (Zer0 Books, 2009) diagnosed a condition in which it had become "easier to imagine an end to the world than an end to capitalism." Fisher argued that capitalist realism is itself a hyperstition — a self-fulfilling sense of future-foreclosure that prevents the construction of alternatives by making them unimaginable.

In Ghosts of My Life (2014) Fisher extended this with the concept of hauntology (after Derrida): contemporary culture haunted by futures that were promised and never arrived, recycling the aesthetics of the 1980s indefinitely because no new future-image is being produced. The exhaustion of mythopoetic capacity is itself politically consequential.

Fisher's late writing — collected posthumously as k-punk (2018) — was attempting to construct counter-hyperstitions, especially around the unfinished Acid Communism manuscript. His suicide in January 2017 left this project incomplete. The work stands as both the most articulate left-wing engagement with hyperstition and a warning about the costs of the underlying conditions on those who try to think against them.

concepts.title: Weaponisation: From Mindfuck to Misinformation
concepts.contentHtml:
The optimistic 1970s reading of Operation Mindfuck assumed that demonstrating the manipulability of the information ecosystem would inoculate the public against credulity. The 2010s and 2020s falsified that hope. The same techniques — fake citations, planted documents, ironic deniability, in-group code — are now standard tools of state-level disinformation operations. Renée DiResta's Invisible Rulers (2024) and Whitney Phillips and Ryan Milner's You Are Here (2020) document the operational continuity.

QAnon (active 2017-present) is the textbook case: an open-ended ARG-shaped conspiracy with cliffhanger drops, in-group decoding rituals, and explicit calls to participate in interpretation. Structurally it is indistinguishable from the hyperstitional design Discordians celebrated in the 1970s. The difference is scale, infrastructure, and consequence — the 6 January 2021 Capitol riot is the ledger entry.

This collapses one of the awkward defences sometimes offered for hyperstition as practice: that it is benign because it is knowing. The same techniques deployed at scale, in adversarial conditions, with state backing, are not benign.

concepts.title: Hyperstition as Cope, Tool, and Diagnosis
concepts.contentHtml:
It is worth taking seriously the criticisms. As cope: the framing can serve to dignify ordinary delusion as avant-garde practice; saying "it is hyperstition" can sometimes just mean "I want to keep believing the fun thing." As tool: explicitly engineering fictions to act on populations is, at scale, a form of manipulation, and the move from "I am studying memes" to "I am deploying memes" carries ethical weight one cannot wave away by citing the CCRU.

As diagnosis: the most defensible use of the concept is probably analytical rather than productive. Recognising that markets, religions, political movements, and AI discourses operate in part through self-fulfilling narrative dynamics improves one's reading of them without requiring participation in their construction.

The cleanest closing question to take from these ten lessons is the one Mark Fisher kept returning to: which future-images are worth helping into existence, and which should one decline to amplify even if amplification would work? Hyperstition, on its honest reading, is not a value-neutral toolkit. Every decision to feed an egregore is a decision about what kind of world one is helping to make.
